setupSteps: Adjust the thigh pad before you sit. Set it so it will rest snugly on the tops of your thighs, a little above the knees, not on the knees or hips. Most guides and machine makers say this stops the weight lifting you out of the seat. A fit that is snug but not painful is the target; one source warns that a gap lets you rise during heavy pulls.

Seat height: set it so your feet are flat on the floor, thighs under the pad, and the bar can be reached with arms fully straight while you stay tall. Some machines have a height guide on the frame; follow the placard. If you are short and your feet dangle, use the lowest seat or a platform; Cybex describes this as keeping full foot contact and a good pelvis position.
Disagreement: one blog suggests a thigh pad position lower down the thigh; others say top of the thigh. FitPlate uses top of the thigh, as the machine makers say.

Wide overhand (the standard): hands on a long bar about 1.5 times shoulder width (est.; guides range from just outside shoulder width up to about double). The 2014 and 2010 EMG studies found similar lat activity across wide and medium grips, so FitPlate starts at the narrow end of "wide": slightly outside shoulder width, thumbs around the bar, wrists straight.
Neutral or close grip: a V-bar or two parallel handles, palms facing each other, hands about shoulder width or a little inside. Many people find this the kindest to the shoulders.
Underhand (reverse): palms facing you, hands just inside shoulder width on a straight bar. It uses the biceps more; start lighter. Avoid it if your elbows or wrists hurt.
Check the bar and cable: look for a frayed cable, a loose snap hook or a stuck pulley; tell staff if the cable looks damaged (inspection steps are common practice; no formal standard was found).

Choose a light start: a load you can pull for 10–12 controlled reps with 3–4 reps left over (est.; see section 7). Push the selector pin fully in so it cannot fall out; check the plate number before you sit.
Machines with a plate-loaded or pin-and-chain stack: ask staff if the plate numbers are unmarked; do not guess.

Sit down: stand next to the seat, take the bar with both hands, then sit back down with your arms straight while the bar rises or stays up; slide your thighs under the pad and plant both feet flat. Several guides say your body weight can help you down; do not let a heavy bar yank your arms up and your shoulders open.

If the load is heavier than your body can hold down: you may need to stand with the bar, use a lighter pin for the first set, or ask staff or a friend to hold the bar down while you sit. Pulling the thigh pad up with your legs to drive the bar down is not recommended: the sources describe the pad as a hold-down, not a pulling aid, and driving with the legs leads to swinging.

Finish the set: after the last rep, let the bar rise slowly with straight arms until the stack nearly touches, then stand up while holding the bar and let it go up gently. Never let go of the bar while it is low and the arms are straight.
If you cannot finish the last rep: do not let the bar fly up. Stand up with the bar in both hands, then return it under control.

Torso: tall and braced, chest up, a slight lean back only. ACE says lean back slightly, no more than about 30 degrees from vertical; other sources suggest about 10–15 degrees (est.; one gym blog); ACE also advises no extra lean during the pull. FitPlate uses an upright or slightly leaning torso (est. 10–15 degrees) with a hard limit of 30 degrees from vertical.
Head and eyes: neck long, chin level, eyes forward, so the bar travels in front of the face and not behind the neck.
Feet: flat on the floor, about hip width, heels slightly behind the knees, not tucked far under the seat (Breaking Muscle).

steps.title: Set the seat, pad and pin
steps.action: Set the seat height and thigh pad as in section 3 and push the pin into a light plate.
steps.visualCheck: Side: pad on top of the thighs, feet flat. Front: knees together under the pad.

steps.title: Take the bar
steps.action: Stand beside the seat, take the bar with both hands at the chosen width, thumbs around it.
steps.visualCheck: Front: hands the same distance from the bar centre; wrists straight.

steps.title: Sit and lock the thighs in
steps.action: Sit down with straight arms; slide the thighs under the pad and plant both feet flat.
steps.feel: Thighs held firmly; arms stretched up.
steps.visualCheck: Side: tall back, tiny lean; seat does not lift.

steps.title: Set the shoulder blades
steps.action: Lift your chest slightly and keep the ribs down; keep the head still.
steps.feel: A stretch under the armpits and back; core braced.
steps.visualCheck: Front: shoulders level, not shrugged to the ears.

steps.title: Start the pull with the shoulder blades
steps.action: Without bending the elbows yet, pull the shoulder blades down and slightly back, as if sliding them into your back pockets.
steps.feel: The back muscles under the armpits working; shoulders moving away from the ears.
steps.visualCheck: Front: the bar moves down a little; the shoulders drop.

steps.title: Pull the elbows down
steps.action: Drive the elbows down and slightly back toward your hips; the bar travels down in front of the face.
steps.feel: The lats pulling the elbows, not the hands or arms.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows point down and slightly forward of the body line; the bar stays level. Side: torso stays still.

steps.title: Touch the upper chest
steps.action: Bring the bar to the upper chest (collarbone area) with the chest up; stop when the elbows start moving backwards, as ACE advises.
steps.feel: A squeeze between the shoulder blades; shoulders down.
steps.visualCheck: Front: bar at collarbone level; elbows beside the ribs. Side: bar in front of the face, never behind the neck.

steps.title: Let the bar rise slowly
steps.action: Straighten the arms under control, letting the shoulder blades rise last.
steps.feel: A stretch in the lats; the stack moves smoothly.
steps.visualCheck: Side: tall torso; plates do not hit the stack. Front: arms straight and even at the top.

steps.title: Repeat, then finish
steps.action: Repeat steps 5–8. After the last rep, stand up holding the bar and let it rise gently (section 3, point 12).
steps.visualCheck: The bar hangs at the top; nothing swings.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling the bar behind the neck
commonMistakes.text: Pulling the bar behind the neck. Why: puts the shoulder in extreme rotation with the neck flexed; no extra lat benefit found. Fix: pull to the upper chest, in front of the face.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning back and swinging like a row
commonMistakes.text: Leaning back and swinging like a row. Why: the pull becomes a heave and the lats do less; ACE advises no extra lean during the pull. Fix: lighter weight, brace the core, lean no more than a slight angle.

commonMistakes.title: Using too much weight and arching the back
commonMistakes.text: Using too much weight and arching the back. Why: the seat lifts, the arms take over and the lower back arches. Fix: lower the pin until you can pull 10–12 clean reps with 3–4 left.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging the shoulders up
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging the shoulders up. Why: the upper trapezius takes over and the neck tightens. Fix: start each rep by pulling the shoulder blades down.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling with the hands (curling the bar)
commonMistakes.text: Pulling with the hands (curling the bar). Why: the biceps do the work and the lats stay switched off. Fix: think "elbows to hips"; lighten the grip.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling the bar below the chest and letting the elbows go far back
commonMistakes.text: Pulling the bar below the chest and letting the elbows go far back. Why: ACE says pulling further adds shoulder stress once the elbows start moving backwards. Fix: stop when the bar touches the upper chest.

commonMistakes.title: Half reps at the top (never fully straightening)
commonMistakes.text: Half reps at the top (never fully straightening). Why: loses the lat stretch. Fix: let the arms straighten fully while the shoulders stay down.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the bar snap up or the stack slam
commonMistakes.text: Letting the bar snap up or the stack slam. Why: jerky loading, noise, and the bar can hit you or a neighbour. Fix: 3-second return; stand up holding the bar at the end.

commonMistakes.title: Thigh pad too loose or too high on the legs
commonMistakes.text: Thigh pad too loose or too high on the legs. Why: the seat lifts or the legs are poorly held. Fix: adjust the pad to sit snugly on the tops of the thighs.

commonMistakes.title: Sitting with the weight too heavy to hold down
commonMistakes.text: Sitting with the weight too heavy to hold down. Why: the bar yanks you up and the shoulders open under load. Fix: lighten the pin or have the bar held while you sit.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems: pull to the front only, with a shorter range, a lighter load and a neutral grip; avoid behind-the-neck; ask a professional.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; breathe out on the pull; moderate loads.
Lower back pain: keep an upright torso and a braced core; no swinging; use a lighter pin or a seated row with chest support if it hurts.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table; ask a professional.
